PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 12

Inflation

In 1981, Alan Guth proposed the theory of inflation as a solution to several of the obvious problems with the standard picture of the Hot Big Bang (in particular the flatness and horizon problems). The detailed physics of inflation are beyond the scope of this course, but the basic principles can be readily understood.

The simplest requirement of inflation is that there was a period when the expansion of the early Universe accelerated very rapidly. At very early times (the tiniest fractions of a second) we therefore require

a¨⁢(t)≫0 (1)

By considering the acceleration equation we see that this is only possible if the contents of the Universe have a negative pressure111 More specifically, a positive acceleration requires p<-13⁢ρ⁢c2.. This is mathematically equivalent to role played by the cosmological constant in the present-day Universe, but on a very different physical scale (by more than 100 orders of magnitude!). We outline the basic physics of inflation here by assuming that this negative pressure can be parametrized as a constant Λi (as this is the simplest case). However, please note that this is not the same as the cosmological constant which is responsible for the accelerating expansion at z=0.

Bearing these caveats in mind, we write the Friedmann equation as:

H2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ-k⁢c2a2+Λi3 (2)

For inflation to occur we require the last term to dominate and, because the matter and curvature terms both decrease as a⁢(t) increases, we can neglect the first two terms and approximate the Friedmann equation in the inflationary epoch as

H2=(a˙a)2≃Λi3(=constant) (3)

Taking square-roots, we find

d⁢ad⁢t=Λi3⁢a (4)

which we then integrate to find

a⁢(t)∝exp⁡(Λi3⁢t) (5)

We therefore see that inflation – in its simplest form – leads to exponential expansion of the early Universe. If Λi is sufficiently large, this results in a⁢(t) increasing by an enormous factor in a very short time.

The solution of the flatness problem can also be understood from this analysis. We previously wrote the Friedmann equation in the following form:

|Ωtot-1|=|k|⁢c2a2⁢H2 (6)

In a matter- or radiation-dominated cosmology a2⁢H2 is a decreasing function of time, so the right-hand-side of Equation 6 increases, and the Universe moves further and further away from Ωtot=1 as it evolves. However, in an epoch of inflation we have a¨>0, which we can write as

dd⁢t⁢(a˙)>0 (7)

We also note that a˙=a⁢H, so we have

dd⁢t⁢(a⁢H)>0 (8)

In this regime the right-hand-side of Equation 6 is a decreasing function of time, so an inflating Universe therefore evolves towards the critical density (i.e., becomes “more flat”) as it expands. For the specific form of inflation described above (Equation 5) we see that

a2⁢(t)∝exp⁡(2⁢Λi3⁢t)∝exp⁡(4⁢Λi3⁢t) (9)

and, as H is constant (Equation 3), we find

|Ωtot-1|∝exp⁡(-4⁢Λi3⁢t) (10)

Inflation therefore results in exponential “damping” of any curvature present in the early Universe, and the flat (k=0) geometry we observe is in fact a natural outcome of any period of rapid inflation. Inflation also means that the scale-factor increases much more rapidly than the horizon distance, which in turn solves the horizon problem (as our observable Universe is now merely a small “patch” which was contained well within the horizon distance prior to inflation).
